name: Grade 11
theme: The sacraments and the moral life in Christ

lessons.title: Christ’s work in the liturgy
lessons.idea: The liturgy is the work of Christ the High Priest and of his Body, the Church. In it God sanctifies us and we worship him; it is the source and summit of the Church’s life. Jesus said true worshipers will worship “in spirit and truth.”
lessons.question: Why is liturgy more than a ritual?
lessons.activity: “Study Sacrosanctum Concilium 7” (40 min). Students read SC 7 and annotate: Christ present in the Mass (minister, species, word, community), the liturgy as the exercise of Christ’s priesthood, the foretaste of heavenly liturgy. Write a paragraph explaining why liturgy is more than ceremony. Read John 4:21–24.
teach: “The liturgy is the participation of the People of God in ‘the work of God’” (CCC 1069). It is the exercise of Christ’s priestly office, in which sanctification is manifested by signs and worship is offered by the whole Body (CCC 1070–1073; SC 7).
Christ is present in the Eucharistic species, in the priest, in the Word, in the gathered community, and in the sacraments (CCC 1088; SC 7).

The liturgy is also the anticipation of the heavenly liturgy (Revelation 4–5; CCC 1090). The Trinity is at work: the Father is source and goal, the Son the mediator, the Spirit prepares and makes present (CCC 1077–1112).
Full, conscious, active participation is the goal (CCC 1071; SC 14).
talk: What does “work of the people” mean?
Why is liturgy more than ritual?
quiz: The liturgy is the work of…|The bishop alone|The choir|The priest alone|Christ and his Body the Church|3|CCC 1070.
“Source and summit” means the liturgy is…|Entertainment|One of many options|A tradition only|Where the Church’s activity flows from and is directed to|3|CCC 1074.
The Trinity’s role in the liturgy includes…|Nothing|Only the Son|Only the Spirit|The Father blesses, the Son redeems, the Spirit sanctifies|3|CCC 1077–1109.
lessons.saint: Pius X: the pope who encouraged frequent Communion and Communion for children.
lessons.mem: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.” (John 4:24)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What does ‘liturgy’ mean?” Greek leitourgia, “public work.” “Whose work is it?” Explore the answer: Christ’s, and ours with him.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how Christ is present in the liturgy in five ways.

lessons.title: Signs that give grace
lessons.idea: Sacraments are efficacious signs of grace instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church. Each uses matter and form, and works ex opere operato: by the power of Christ’s action, not the minister’s holiness. They continue Jesus’ touching and healing in the Gospels.
lessons.question: What does “ex opere operato” mean?
lessons.activity: “Matter and form chart” (35 min). Students create a chart for the seven sacraments: matter, form, minister, effect. Identify the “visible sign” and “invisible grace.” Include sacramentals as distinct. Discuss why God works through material things.
teach: “Sacraments are efficacious signs of grace, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church” (CCC 1131). They “make present” what they signify (CCC 1084).
Ex opere operato: the sacrament works by the very fact of the action’s being performed (CCC 1128). This protects us from the minister’s unworthiness; the fruit depends on the recipient’s disposition.
Matter and form come from the early Church’s theology; matter is the thing (water, oil), form the words. The minister must intend what the Church does (CCC 1256, 1584).
Sacramentals (blessings, holy water, medals) are sacred signs instituted by the Church that prepare us for grace (CCC 1667–1679).
talk: What does ex opere operato protect?
quiz: Ex opere operato means…|It depends on feeling|The recipient earns it|The minister’s holiness works it|The sacrament works by Christ’s action|3|CCC 1128.
A sacramental is…|A relic only|A superstition|A sacrament|A sacred sign instituted by the Church|3|CCC 1667.
Fruitful reception requires…|Faith and proper disposition|Age|Understanding of Latin|Wealth|0|CCC 1131.
lessons.life: Chart matter, form and minister for the seven sacraments.
lessons.saint: Thomas Aquinas: the Dominican friar who wrote the Summa Theologiae and hymns for the Eucharist.
lessons.mem: “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.” (Mark 5:34)
lessons.hook: Read Mark 5:25–34, the woman who touches Jesus’ cloak. Ask: “What went out from Jesus?” Sacraments are touch points of his power.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain ex opere operato and complete a matter/form chart for three sacraments.

lessons.title: Disposition and fruitfulness
lessons.idea: Sacraments bear fruit according to the faith and disposition of those who receive them. Faith, repentance and desire open us to grace, while indifference or insincerity can block it. Preparation and thanksgiving matter.
lessons.question: Why are dispositions important?
lessons.activity: “Reflect on your reception” (35 min). Students privately reflect on the last time they received a sacrament: How did I prepare? How attentive was I? How did it change me? Write a short plan for a deeper reception. No sharing required, only volunteers.
teach: The sacraments confer grace, but it bears fruit according to dispositions (CCC 1128, 1131). Faith is required: they are “sacraments of faith” (CCC 1122–1126).
Hebrews 11:6: “without faith it is impossible to please him.” Repentance is needed for Eucharist and Confirmation if in mortal sin (CCC 1415).
Obstacles: unrepented mortal sin, indifference, a faithless approach. Fruits increase with devotion, as with spiritual preparation (CCC 1123–1126).
Sacramental life is the normal means of spiritual growth, but God’s grace is not limited to them (CCC 1257).
talk: What is the role of faith?
How can we participate more fully?
quiz: Sacramental character is received in…|The Eucharist|Penance|Baptism, Confirmation, Holy Orders|Matrimony|2|CCC 1121.
Participation means primarily…|Singing only|Outward activity only|Standing only|Interior engagement|3|SC 14.
Sacraments bear fruit in those who…|Are wealthy|Are well disposed|Are famous|Are old|1|CCC 1128.
lessons.life: Prepare for the next Mass by praying the readings beforehand.
lessons.saint: Pius X: the pope who encouraged frequent Communion and Communion for children.
misc: “The sacraments work regardless of my attitude.”
“I must be perfect before I receive.”
lessons.mem: “And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.” (Hebrews 11:6)
lessons.hook: Hold out a gift and ask a volunteer to receive it with arms crossed. “The gift is real but is it received?” Introduce disposition.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how disposition affects sacramental fruit and give an example.

lessons.title: Baptism
lessons.idea: Baptism is new birth in water and the Spirit. Its matter is water; its form, “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” It forgives original and personal sin, makes us children of God and incorporates us into the Church. Infants are baptized; those who die before Baptism can be saved by desire or blood.
lessons.question: Why baptize infants?
lessons.activity: “Rite and objections” (40 min). Students study the Rite of Baptism and then prepare answers to: “Why baptize infants?”, “Isn’t it just symbolic?”, “What about the unbaptized?” Use CCC 1213–1284 and Scripture (Acts 16:15, 33; Colossians 2:11–12).
teach: Baptism is the “gateway to life in the Spirit” and the door to the other sacraments (CCC 1213). Its effects: forgiveness of sin, new birth, incorporation into Christ and the Church, an indelible character (CCC 1262–1274).
Minister: bishop, priest, deacon; in necessity anyone with the right intention (CCC 1256). Baptism by water is ordinary; baptism of blood (martyrdom) and desire also bring salvation (CCC 1258–1260).
Infant Baptism: the Church has done so since apostolic times; it rests on the gratuity of grace (CCC 1250–1252).
The Church entrusts unbaptized infants to God’s mercy (CCC 1261).
quiz: The form of Baptism is…|“I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”|“Peace”|“Amen”|“Be blessed”|0|CCC 1240.
Baptism of desire is…|Not recognized|Salvation of a catechumen who dies before Baptism|A rite|A second baptism|1|CCC 1259.
Baptism’s effects include…|Citizenship|Nothing visible|Forgiveness of all sin|A new name only|2|CCC 1263.
lessons.saint: Augustine: who searched for truth for years before writing, “Our heart is restless until it rests in you.”
misc: “Infants are baptized without their consent, so it’s invalid.”
“Baptism guarantees heaven regardless of how you live.”
lessons.mem: “Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” (John 3:5)
lessons.hook: Read John 3:1–8. Ask: “Why did Nicodemus misunderstand ‘born again’?” Compare to Baptism.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the effects of Baptism and defend infant Baptism.

lessons.title: Confirmation
lessons.idea: Confirmation completes baptismal grace by sealing us with the Holy Spirit. The bishop lays on hands and anoints with chrism, saying “Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.” We receive an increase of the Spirit’s gifts and a call to witness.
lessons.question: What do we receive?
lessons.activity: “Write a reflection” (35 min). Students write a reflection on the meaning of chrism (olive oil and balsam, consecrated by the bishop on Holy Thursday), the gifts, and their own call to witness. They answer: “What would it look like to live as sealed by the Spirit?”
teach: Confirmation, with Baptism and Eucharist, is a sacrament of initiation (CCC 1285). The rite includes renewal of baptismal promises, laying on of hands and anointing (CCC 1297–1301).

It imprints an indelible character and increases the gifts of the Spirit (CCC 1303–1305). The bishop is the original minister; priests confirm by delegation, especially in the Eastern Churches and in adult initiation (CCC 1312–1314).
Candidates must be baptized and in a state of grace; a sponsor helps (CCC 1306–1311).
Address the question of age: practice varies. The sacrament is not a “graduation” but a beginning of mission.
quiz: The ordinary minister is…|The bishop|A layperson|A priest only|A deacon|0|CCC 1313.
The matter is…|Ashes|Bread|Chrism and laying on of hands|Water|2|CCC 1300.
Confirmation increases…|Age|Wealth|The gifts of the Holy Spirit|Honor|2|CCC 1303.
lessons.life: Write a reflection on what the Spirit is calling you to.
lessons.saint: Philip Neri: the joyful “apostle of Rome,” who gathered young people for prayer and service.
misc: “Confirmation is only for those who choose it.”
“Confirmation gives gifts we did not already have at Baptism.”
lessons.mem: “Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.” (Rite of Confirmation)
lessons.hook: Read Acts 8:14–17. Ask: “What was missing after Philip’s baptisms? Why did Peter and John come?” Introduce the ancient practice of laying on of hands.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the rite, its effects and the role of the bishop.

lessons.title: Eucharist
lessons.idea: The Eucharist is the source and summit of the Christian life: institution at the Last Supper, Real Presence, sacrifice and banquet. John 6, Luke 22 and 1 Corinthians 11 are central texts. Christ gives himself under the appearances of bread and wine.
lessons.question: Why did Jesus say flesh?
lessons.activity: “Analyze John 6” (40 min). Students read John 6:22–71 and outline: the sign (bread), the discourse (bread from heaven, flesh and blood), the reaction. Compare with Luke 22:19–20 and 1 Corinthians 11:23–29. Write a one-page explanation of the Real Presence and how Scripture supports it.
teach: The Eucharist is “the source and summit of the Christian life” (CCC 1324). Institution: Last Supper (Luke 22; CCC 1337–1340).
The Real Presence: Christ is present “whole and entire… body and blood, soul and divinity” (CCC 1374). Transubstantiation names the change of substance (CCC 1376–1377).
The Eucharist is memorial, sacrifice, communion and thanksgiving (CCC 1356–1372). Fruits: union with Christ, forgiveness of venial sin, unity of the Church (CCC 1391–1397).
Paul warns that eating unworthily brings judgment (1 Corinthians 11:27–29). We prepare by faith, Confession as needed, fasting and reverence (CCC 1385–1387).
talk: Why did Jesus say flesh and blood?
How did early Christians treat the Eucharist?
quiz: Transubstantiation is…|Memorial only|Change of the whole substance|Mixed bread and body|Symbol only|1|CCC 1376.
The Eucharist unites us to…|Only ourselves|The priest|Nobody|Christ and the Church|3|CCC 1396.
Ignatius of Antioch wrote that the Eucharist is…|A meal|A symbol|The flesh of our Savior|A rule|2|Smyrnaeans 7.
lessons.life: Read Ignatius and Justin on the Eucharist.
lessons.saint: Carlo Acutis: a teenager who loved the Eucharist, used computers to share the faith and died at 15.
misc: “Communion is a reward for the good.”
lessons.mem: “My flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink.” (John 6:55)
lessons.hook: Read John 6:51–60. Ask: “Why did many disciples leave? What did Jesus do?” He did not take back his words.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the Real Presence using Scripture and Church teaching.

units.title: Healing: Reconciliation and Anointing
units.eq: How does Christ heal and forgive?

lessons.title: Sin and mercy
lessons.idea: Sin wounds our relationship with God, ourselves and others; mercy heals. Psalm 51 is the model of repentance: “Have mercy on me, O God… create in me a clean heart.” The Church distinguishes mortal and venial sin and always offers forgiveness.
lessons.question: What is sin?
lessons.activity: “Study Psalm 51” (35 min). Students annotate Psalm 51 in sections: confession (1–6), plea for cleansing (7–12), promise to witness (13–17). Note the context (2 Samuel 12). Write a personal version of the psalm for today.
teach: Sin is “an offense against reason, truth and right conscience” and against God (CCC 1849–1851). Mortal sin requires grave matter, full knowledge and deliberate consent (CCC 1857); venial sin weakens charity (CCC 1862–1863).
The root of sin is in the heart (CCC 1853–1854). Capital sins are vices that give rise to others (CCC 1866).
God’s mercy is greater: Jesus forgives sinners (Luke 15). “Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20; CCC 1847).
Address scrupulosity with care; the remedy is trust and spiritual direction.
quiz: Sin is…|A mistake|A habit|An offense against God|A feeling|2|CCC 1850.
Venial sin…|Is nothing|Is permitted|Destroys grace|Wounds love|3|CCC 1855.
Psalm 51 is a prayer of…|Thanksgiving|Praise|Repentance|Celebration|2|Psalm 51.
lessons.saint: David: a shepherd and king who sinned, repented and wrote many of the Psalms.
lessons.mem: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10)
lessons.hook: Read Psalm 51:1–4. Ask: “What does David admit? What does he ask?” He doesn’t excuse himself; he appeals to mercy.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the effects of sin and the shape of repentance in Psalm 51.

lessons.title: Confession
lessons.idea: In the Sacrament of Penance, a penitent confesses sins to a priest, who gives absolution in Christ’s name. The sacrament requires contrition, confession, satisfaction and absolution. The seal of confession is inviolable. Frequent Confession deepens conversion.
lessons.question: Why confess to a priest?
lessons.activity: “Respond to an objection” (40 min). Students prepare responses to: “Why confess to a priest, not directly to God?”, “Who is the priest to forgive?”, “Isn’t it embarrassing?” Use John 20:23, 2 Corinthians 5:18–20 and James 5:16. Practice a respectful dialogue.
teach: The sacrament goes by many names: Penance, Reconciliation, Confession, Conversion (CCC 1423–1424). Acts of the penitent: contrition, confession, satisfaction (CCC 1450–1460).
The priest acts in persona Christi (CCC 1461–1467). He is bound by the sacramental seal, absolutely and without exception (CCC 1467).
Mortal sins must be confessed in kind and number; the faithful are obliged to confess at least once a year (CCC 1456–1457, 2042). Frequent Confession is recommended (CCC 1458).
Effects: reconciliation with God and the Church, remission of eternal punishment, peace of conscience (CCC 1468–1470).
quiz: Perfect contrition arises from…|Love of God|Fear|Embarrassment|Habit|0|CCC 1452.
The seal of confession is…|Negotiable|Optional|Broken by law|Inviolable|3|CCC 1467.
Absolution is…|The priest’s words forgiving in Christ’s name|A suggestion|A blessing|A prayer only|0|CCC 1449.
lessons.life: Make a good Confession and write a thank-you prayer.
lessons.saint: John Vianney: the village priest who heard confessions up to sixteen hours a day.
misc: “I can just confess privately to God.”
lessons.mem: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, and will forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)
lessons.hook: Read John 20:21–23. Ask: “Why would Jesus breathe on the apostles and give them this power?” Ask students to compare to Jesus forgiving sins in Mark 2.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe the four parts of the sacrament and answer one objection.

lessons.title: Anointing of the Sick
lessons.idea: In the Anointing of the Sick, the priest anoints with oil and prays for strength, forgiveness and comfort in serious illness or old age. It prepares the soul for healing or for passing to the Father. It may be repeated.
lessons.question: Who may receive it?
lessons.activity: “Interview a chaplain” (40 min). Invite a hospital or hospice chaplain, or watch an interview. Prepare questions: What do you see in suffering? How do you minister to the dying? What do families need? Write a reflection on how to accompany the sick.
teach: The sacrament is for those seriously ill or weakened by age (CCC 1514–1515). Its effects: uniting the sick person with the Passion, strength, peace, forgiveness, and sometimes physical healing (CCC 1520–1523).
The minister is a priest. The matter is oil blessed by the bishop (or by the priest in need), and the form is the prayer (CCC 1519, 1512–1513).
Viaticum, Communion for the dying, is the “food for the journey” (CCC 1524–1525). Together with Penance and Anointing, these are the last sacraments.
It is not “last rites” only. Encourage receiving it before surgery or in serious illness.
talk: How do we accompany the sick?
quiz: Viaticum is…|Confession|Anointing|Eucharist for the dying|Funeral|2|CCC 1517.
Anointing may be received…|By priests only|Once|Never|More than once|3|CCC 1515.
The matter is…|Ashes|Salt|Oil of the sick|Water|2|CCC 1513.
lessons.life: Visit a hospital or nursing home.
lessons.saint: Camillus: a former soldier who founded an order to care for the sick.
misc: “Last rites are only for the dying.”
lessons.mem: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.” (James 5:14)
lessons.hook: Read James 5:14–15. Ask: “What do the elders do? What is promised?” Notice anointing, prayer, faith, forgiveness and healing.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain who may receive the sacrament, its effects and how to support the sick.

units.title: Service: Orders and Matrimony
units.eq: How do sacraments build the Church?

lessons.title: Holy Orders
lessons.idea: Holy Orders confers sacred power to teach, sanctify and govern in Christ’s name. It has three degrees: bishop, priest, deacon. The ministerial priesthood differs in essence from the common priesthood of the faithful. The Church ordains only baptized men, following Christ’s choice of the Twelve.
lessons.question: Why only men?
lessons.activity: “Study CCC 1577 and Ordinatio Sacerdotalis” (40 min). Students read CCC 1577 and John Paul II’s Ordinatio Sacerdotalis (1994): the arguments (Christ’s choice, apostolic practice, Church’s constant Tradition) and what it does not say (women’s dignity). Debate respectfully, with guidelines.
teach: Holy Orders is the sacrament through which the mission entrusted by Christ to his apostles continues until the end of time (CCC 1536). The three degrees: episcopate, presbyterate, diaconate (CCC 1554).
The priest acts in persona Christi capitis (CCC 1548). Ordination imprints an indelible character (CCC 1582).
“Only a baptized man (vir) validly receives sacred ordination” (CCC 1577). Jesus freely chose men for the Twelve; the Church has no authority to change this (CCC 1577–1578; John Paul II).
Affirm women’s dignity and roles in the Church (CCC 2334–2336). Distinguish equal dignity from identical function.
quiz: The priest acts…|In persona Christi|Alone|As a teacher only|As a king|0|CCC 1548.
The three degrees are…|Teacher, doctor, lawyer|Bishop, priest, deacon|Pope, cardinal, priest|Monk, nun, lay|1|CCC 1554.
Ordination is for…|Only celibates|Anyone|Women|Baptized men|3|CCC 1577.
lessons.saint: John Vianney: the village priest who heard confessions up to sixteen hours a day.
misc: “The exclusion of women is only cultural.”
lessons.mem: “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.” (Hebrews 5:6)
lessons.hook: Read Hebrews 5:1–10. Ask: “What does the high priest do? How is Christ the perfect High Priest?” The priesthood participates in his.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the three degrees of Orders and the Church’s reasons for ordaining only men.

lessons.title: Marriage as a sacrament
lessons.idea: Marriage is a covenant of love between a baptized man and woman, established by God and raised by Christ to a sacrament. Its properties are unity and indissolubility; its ends are the good of the spouses and the procreation and education of children. Consent makes the marriage.
lessons.question: Why is marriage indissoluble?
lessons.activity: “Debate” (40 min). Teams debate a proposition such as “Marriage should be seen as a permanent covenant, not a contract renewable at will.” They use Scripture (Genesis 2:24; Mark 10:6–9), natural law and experience. Conclude with each student writing how a covenant differs from a contract.
teach: Marriage is “a covenant by which a man and a woman establish between themselves a partnership of the whole of life” (CCC 1601; Canon 1055). The consent of the spouses makes it (CCC 1626–1628).
The goods of marriage: unity, indissolubility, fidelity, openness to children (CCC 1643–1654). A valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved (CCC 1640).
Impediments and annulment: the Church can declare that a union was never valid (CCC 1629–1637; see the lesson on annulment).
The spouses are the ministers; the Church’s witness is essential. Marriage preparation matters.
quiz: Marriage is a covenant of…|Two friends|Families|A man and a woman|States|2|CCC 1601.
The couple are the ministers because…|The parents|The witnesses|Consent makes marriage|The priest only|2|CCC 1623.
An annulment declares a marriage…|Forgiven|Ended|Dissolved|Never valid|3|CCC 1629.
lessons.saint: Louis and Zélie Martin: parents of Thérèse, canonized together as a married couple.
lessons.mem: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.” (Genesis 2:24)
lessons.hook: Read Ephesians 5:25–32 and Genesis 2:24. Ask: “What does it mean that marriage reflects Christ and the Church?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to state the goods of marriage and explain why consent is essential.

lessons.title: Family and vocation
lessons.idea: The Christian family is the domestic church: a school of faith, prayer and love where children first learn about God. Parents are the first teachers. The Holy Family, especially Joseph’s fidelity and Mary’s trust, is the model.
lessons.question: What makes a home holy?
lessons.activity: “Plan a family prayer” (35 min). Students plan a simple family prayer pattern (meal blessing, bedtime blessing, Sunday Mass, seasonal customs like the Advent wreath) that suits their home. They write a short script. They also design an act of service for their family.
teach: The family is “the domestic church” (CCC 1655–1658; Lumen Gentium 11). Parents are the first heralds of the faith (CCC 2223–2226).
The family is the original cell of social life (CCC 2207). Duties: children honor parents (CCC 2214–2220); parents educate and respect their children (CCC 2221–2231).
Families come in many shapes; the Church cares for single parents, blended families and those in difficulty. Pope Francis’ Amoris Laetitia accompanies families with mercy.
Prayer and practice at home matter more than lessons.
talk: What is the role of parents?
quiz: The family is called the…|School|Business|Domestic church|Club|2|CCC 1655.
Parents are the…|Last teachers|Enemies|First educators|Optional|2|CCC 1653.
Family prayer…|Is old|Is private|Is optional|Builds communion|3|CCC 2205.
lessons.saint: Gianna Molla: a doctor and mother who chose her baby’s life over her own.
misc: “Only perfect families can be a domestic church.”
lessons.mem: “As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.” (Joshua 24:15)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 2:41–52. Ask: “What does this family do together? What does it suffer?” A real family with real worry.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe three habits of a domestic church and commit to one.

lessons.title: The dignity of the person and the Beatitudes
lessons.idea: Every person is made in God’s image and called to beatitude: to share in God’s own happiness. The Beatitudes name the attitudes and actions that lead there, and they answer the natural desire for happiness.
lessons.question: Where is happiness found?
lessons.activity: “Reflect” (30 min). Students choose one Beatitude and write on the cost, the promise and a person they know who lives it. They list one decision this week that expresses it. Class shares anonymously.
teach: Human dignity: created in the image of God, with intellect and will (CCC 1700–1709). Our vocation is beatitude (CCC 1718–1719).
The Beatitudes depict Christ’s own character and the actions of the disciple (CCC 1716–1717). They reorient our desires toward God (CCC 1723–1729).
Happiness is found only in God (CCC 1718, 1723). Thomas Aquinas: happiness is the vision of God.
The moral life starts with who we are and what we are for, not with a list of prohibitions.
quiz: Human dignity comes from…|Wealth|Achievements|Citizenship|Being made in God’s image|3|CCC 1700.
We are made for…|Beatitude|Success|Fame|Pleasure|0|CCC 1718.
The Beatitudes are…|A prophecy|A rule list|The way to happiness|A law|2|CCC 1716.
lessons.saint: Francis: who gave up wealth to follow Christ in poverty and joy and loved creation.
misc: “Morality is just a list of don’ts.”
lessons.mem: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” (Matthew 5:8)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do you think is the secret to being happy?” List answers. Read Matthew 5:1–12.
lessons.assess: Ask students to link human dignity to the Beatitudes in a short paragraph.

lessons.title: Freedom, conscience and natural law
lessons.idea: Freedom is the power to act for the good; conscience is the judgment of reason about right and wrong; natural law is the participation of rational creatures in God’s eternal law. These three are the foundations of moral life.
lessons.question: What is natural law?
lessons.activity: “Discussion” (40 min). Students explore: Is there a moral law all humans can know? Evidence (universal prohibitions on murder, theft), objections (cultural relativism), responses. Compare with the Decalogue. Draw a diagram connecting freedom, conscience and natural law.
teach: Freedom is the power to act or not act (CCC 1731). It grows as we choose the good; sin diminishes it (CCC 1739–1742).
Conscience: “a judgment of reason by which the human person recognizes the moral quality of a concrete act” (CCC 1778). It must be formed and followed (CCC 1783–1790).
Natural law: “nothing other than the light of understanding placed in us by God” (Aquinas; CCC 1954–1960). It is universal and unchangeable, the basis for human rights.
The Old Law and New Law complete natural law (CCC 1961–1974).
talk: How does it relate to conscience?
quiz: Natural law is…|A church rule|Moral law known by reason|A civil law|A law of physics|1|CCC 1954.
Conscience must be…|Formed|Ignored|Silent|Trusted blindly|0|CCC 1783.
Freedom is…|For power|For escape|For the good|For choosing anything|2|CCC 1731.
lessons.life: Read about natural law in CCC.
lessons.saint: Aquinas: the Dominican friar who wrote the Summa Theologiae and hymns for the Eucharist.
lessons.mem: “They show that what the law requires is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness.” (Romans 2:15)
lessons.hook: Read Romans 2:14–16. Ask: “How can people who do not know the law still do what it requires?” Introduce natural law.
lessons.assess: Ask students to define freedom, conscience and natural law and show how they connect.

lessons.title: Sin, virtue and grace
lessons.idea: Virtue is a habit of doing good; sin is the opposite. Grace is God’s free gift that heals and elevates us. Together they form the dynamic of the moral life: God’s grace, our response, virtues that grow, and the fruits of the Spirit.
lessons.question: How do we grow in virtue?
lessons.activity: “Make a plan” (35 min). Students identify one virtue to cultivate and one vice to resist. They design a habit plan: a daily practice, a support person, a prayer, a measure. They reflect on how grace will help.
teach: Virtues are habits of the soul (CCC 1803). The human virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance (CCC 1805–1809). Theological virtues: faith, hope, charity (CCC 1812–1829).
Grace is “favor, the free and undeserved help that God gives us” (CCC 1996). Sanctifying grace makes us holy; actual grace helps in particular acts (CCC 2000).
The gifts and fruits of the Holy Spirit complete the virtues (CCC 1830–1832). Merit is possible because grace is already at work (CCC 2006–2011).
Vice is the habit of sin. The seven capital sins and their remedies are a classic guide.
quiz: Cardinal virtues are…|Joy, peace, patience|Chastity, poverty, obedience|Prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance|Faith, hope, love|2|CCC 1805.
Theological virtues are…|Humility, patience|Patience, kindness|Faith, hope, charity|Courage, wisdom|2|CCC 1813.
Grace is…|A wage|A rule|A free gift|An ability|2|CCC 1996.
lessons.saint: Aquinas: the Dominican friar who wrote the Summa Theologiae and hymns for the Eucharist.
lessons.mem: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)
lessons.hook: Read Galatians 5:22–23. Ask: “How do you recognize a person of virtue?” By the fruit, not just the rules.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe how grace and virtue work together with an example.

units.title: The Commandments I: love of God

lessons.title: First commandment
lessons.idea: The first commandment, “You shall have no other gods before me,” commands faith, hope and charity and forbids superstition, idolatry, divination, atheism and tempting God. Worship belongs to God alone.
lessons.question: What are modern idols?
lessons.activity: “Reflect” (30 min). Students list modern “idols” and the signs of idolatry (time, devotion, sacrifices, identity). They write a short examination of their own lives: What could take first place in my heart? What is my plan to keep God first?
teach: The first commandment calls us to believe in God, hope in him and love him above all (CCC 2084–2094). Adoration, prayer, sacrifice and keeping promises are acts of worship (CCC 2096–2103).

Sins against it: doubt, unbelief, heresy, apostasy, schism (CCC 2088–2089); presumption, despair (CCC 2091–2092); superstition, idolatry, divination, magic, sacrilege, simony (CCC 2110–2128); atheism, agnosticism (CCC 2123–2128).
Images are not forbidden: Christ’s Incarnation makes holy images possible (CCC 2129–2132).
Idolatry today may take the form of power, pleasure, money or ideologies (CCC 2113).
quiz: The first commandment forbids…|Stealing|Idolatry|Killing|Lying|1|CCC 2112.
Superstition is…|Healthy faith|Prayer|Hope|Misdirected religious feeling|3|CCC 2110.
Atheism is…|Faith|Doubt|Prayer|Denial of God|3|CCC 2123.
lessons.saint: Thomas More: the lawyer and statesman who told the truth to a king and died for his conscience.
lessons.mem: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might.” (Deuteronomy 6:5)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do people give their lives to?” (fame, money, success, relationships). Read Exodus 20:3 and introduce idolatry as putting a created good in God’s place.
lessons.assess: Ask students to identify three sins against the first commandment and give a modern example of idolatry.

lessons.title: Second and third commandments
lessons.idea: The second commandment commands reverence for God’s name, forbidding blasphemy, perjury and the misuse of oaths. The third commandment commands keeping the Lord’s Day holy by participating in Mass and resting from unnecessary work.
lessons.question: How do we keep Sunday?
lessons.activity: “Plan a Sunday” (35 min). Students plan a model Sunday that includes Mass, rest, family, service and leisure. They note obstacles (sports, work, screens) and solutions. Write a Sunday commitment.
teach: The second commandment: God’s name is holy (CCC 2142–2149). Blasphemy, profanity, false oaths and cursing are sins (CCC 2148–2155). Using God’s name in prayer and blessing honors it.
The third: Sunday is the Lord’s Day, commemorating the Resurrection (CCC 2174–2176). Sunday Mass is obligatory (CCC 2180–2183); rest, family, charity and leisure belong to the day (CCC 2184–2188).
Holy days of obligation in the United States: Mary Mother of God, Ascension, Assumption, All Saints, Immaculate Conception, Christmas (with the usual exceptions) (CCC 2043).
Excuses: illness, caring for infants and similar serious reasons (CCC 2181).
quiz: The Lord’s Day is…|Monday|Friday|Sunday|Saturday|2|CCC 2174.
Blasphemy is…|Honest oaths|Words against God|Jokes|Silence|1|CCC 2148.
On Sunday we…|Work|Worship and rest|Play only|Shop|1|CCC 2185.
lessons.life: Keep Sunday as a day of rest.
lessons.saint: John Paul II: the pope who taught on love and the body, and who prayed with leaders of many faiths.
lessons.mem: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.” (Exodus 20:8)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would you think if someone used your name as a curse?” Read Exodus 20:7–11. God’s name is holy.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain why God’s name is holy and how to keep Sunday holy.

lessons.title: Prayer as response
lessons.idea: Prayer is the response of the human heart to God, a living relationship. Whether vocal, meditative or contemplative, prayer is a gift God offers, and a battle we must fight. Luke 11:1: “Lord, teach us to pray.”
lessons.question: How do we pray?
lessons.activity: “Pray a Psalm” (35 min). Students pray Psalm 63 or 130 slowly in different ways: aloud together, silently, as a dialogue. Afterwards, they write a short reflection on what the Psalm says about prayer, and how they can pray it again this week.
teach: Prayer is “the raising of one’s mind and heart to God” (CCC 2559). It is a response to God’s initiative: “God thirsts that we may thirst for him” (CCC 2560).
Forms: blessing, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, praise (CCC 2626–2643). Expressions: vocal, meditation, contemplation (CCC 2700–2724).
The battle of prayer: distraction, dryness, discouragement, acedia. Persevere (CCC 2725–2745).
The place of prayer: the home, church, small spaces, nature. Time: daily, with the Church (CCC 2691–2699).
quiz: Prayer is…|A technique|A chore|A mood|Raising the mind and heart to God|3|CCC 2559.
The forms include…|Games|Debates|Blessing, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, praise|Rules|2|CCC 2626.
Prayer requires…|Perfect silence|Perseverance|Latin|A church|1|CCC 2742.
lessons.saint: Teresa: a Carmelite who reformed her order and taught that prayer is friendship with God.
misc: “If I am distracted, I am not praying.”
lessons.mem: “Lord, teach us to pray.” (Luke 11:1)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 11:1. Ask: “Why did the disciples ask this question? What did they see in Jesus’ prayer?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to name forms and expressions of prayer and an obstacle.

units.title: The Commandments II: love of neighbor

lessons.title: Life and chastity
lessons.idea: The fifth commandment protects the dignity of human life from conception to natural death; the sixth, with the ninth, protects the dignity of the person in sexuality through chastity. Both defend persons from being used.
lessons.question: What does the Church teach about chastity?
lessons.activity: “Respectful conversation” (40 min). With ground rules (listen, no mocking, optional sharing), students discuss: How do culture and media portray sex and violence? What does a life-giving view look like? Individually write a personal commitment to treat others as persons, not objects.
teach: The fifth commandment forbids murder and teaches respect for human life (CCC 2258–2317). Abortion, euthanasia, suicide are grave offenses (CCC 2270–2283). Legitimate defense, war and the death penalty have strict limits (CCC 2263–2267, 2307–2317).
Chastity is the integration of sexuality within the person (CCC 2337). All are called to chastity according to their state: married, single, consecrated (CCC 2348–2350).

Offenses against chastity include lust, masturbation, pornography, fornication, prostitution, rape, adultery, homosexual acts, contraception (CCC 2351–2357, 2380–2391). Teach with charity and clarity.
Forgiveness, mercy and help are always available (CCC 1429).
talk: How do we speak with compassion?
quiz: Life is sacred…|From conception to natural death|Never|From birth|From age 18|0|CCC 2270.
Chastity is…|Silence|Fear|Repression|Integration of sexuality|3|CCC 2337.
Murder is…|Gravely wrong|A right|Legal|Sometimes permissible|0|CCC 2268.
lessons.saint: Gianna Molla: a doctor and mother who chose her baby’s life over her own.
lessons.mem: “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.” (Genesis 1:27)
lessons.hook: Read Psalm 139:13–16 and Genesis 1:27. Ask: “How does it change how you treat people if each is made in the image of God?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain why life and chastity are connected to human dignity.

lessons.title: Justice and truth
lessons.idea: The seventh commandment forbids theft and commands justice in property, work and the care of the poor; the eighth commands truthfulness and forbids lying, calumny and detraction. Together they build trust in society.
lessons.question: How can we practice honesty?
lessons.activity: “Case studies” (40 min). Students study cases: cheating on a test, using pirated media, a business with unfair wages, spreading a rumor, keeping a secret. For each: which commandment, what justice requires, what repair is needed (restitution, apology).
teach: The seventh commandment: respect for others’ goods; the universal destination of goods and private property (CCC 2401–2418). Sins: theft, fraud, unjust wages, gambling abuse, cheating (CCC 2408–2414).
The Church’s social teaching: just wages, care for creation, solidarity with the poor (CCC 2426–2463).
The eighth: truth, witness and honesty (CCC 2464–2513). Sins: lying, perjury, rash judgment, detraction, calumny, flattery, boasting (CCC 2475–2487). Professional secrecy and the seal are protected.
Restitution is required when we harm others (CCC 2487).
quiz: The eighth commandment concerns…|Marriage|Property|Life|Truth|3|CCC 2464.
Calumny is…|Silence|Gossip|Truth|Lying to harm reputation|3|CCC 2477.
Restitution is…|Ignoring|Punishing|Repairing injustice|Hiding|2|CCC 2412.
lessons.saint: Thomas More: the lawyer and statesman who told the truth to a king and died for his conscience.
misc: “Small lies and small thefts don’t matter.”
lessons.mem: “Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.” (Amos 5:24)
lessons.hook: Read Amos 5:24. Ask: “How does a society fall apart when no one tells the truth or respects property?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to analyze a scenario using the seventh and eighth commandments.

lessons.title: Desire and detachment
lessons.idea: The ninth and tenth commandments reach the heart: purity of heart and detachment from possessions. “Blessed are the pure in heart.” They teach us to guard desires and to be generous and content.
lessons.question: What does purity of heart mean?
lessons.activity: “Reflection” (30 min). Students journal on: What do I envy? What do I covet? How do I guard my heart (media, friendships, gratitude)? They choose one practical step toward purity of heart and one toward generosity.
teach: The ninth commandment: purity of heart; battles against lust through modesty, discipline of the senses and prayer (CCC 2514–2533). The tenth: detachment from riches and envy (CCC 2534–2557).
Envy is sadness at another’s good; avarice, a desire for wealth. The remedy is gratitude, generosity and trust in providence (CCC 2538–2540, 2544–2547).
“Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3) points to the freedom of detachment. “Where your treasure is, there will be your heart also” (Matthew 6:21).
Modesty protects intimacy and human dignity (CCC 2521–2524).
talk: How do we grow in detachment?
quiz: Purity of heart sees…|Money|Self|God|Fame|2|Matthew 5:8.
Envy is…|Anger|Joy|Sadness at another’s good|Pride|2|CCC 2539.
Detachment is…|Poverty only|Freedom from disordered attachments|Laziness|Fear|1|CCC 2544.
lessons.life: Practice detachment: fast from a pleasure.
lessons.saint: Francis: who gave up wealth to follow Christ in poverty and joy and loved creation.
lessons.mem: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” (Matthew 5:8)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 5:8 and 5:28. Ask: “Why does Jesus say sin begins in the heart?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe the difference between wants and covetousness and one remedy.

units.title: Social teaching and conscience in action
units.eq: What does it mean to love in society?

lessons.title: Human dignity and the common good
lessons.idea: Catholic social teaching begins with the dignity of the human person, who is the foundation, cause and goal of social life. The common good is the sum of conditions that allow people to flourish. Subsidiarity and participation protect freedom.
lessons.question: What is the common good?
lessons.activity: “Case study” (40 min). Present a local issue (a closing factory, a refugee family, a neighborhood without a grocery store). Students apply the principles: dignity, common good, subsidiarity, participation, solidarity. Propose practical actions and who should act.
teach: Society exists for the person (CCC 1877–1885). The common good: “the sum total of social conditions which allow people… to reach their fulfillment more fully and more easily” (CCC 1906).
Subsidiarity: larger bodies should not take over what smaller communities can do (CCC 1883–1885). Participation allows all to contribute (CCC 1913–1917).
Authority serves the common good (CCC 1897–1904). The state must protect human rights (CCC 1907–1912).
Rerum Novarum (1891), Quadragesimo Anno, Mater et Magistra, Gaudium et Spes, Centesimus Annus and Laudato Si’ develop these themes.
talk: What is the role of authority?
quiz: The common good is…|Majority benefit|Conditions allowing all to flourish|Wealth|Law|1|CCC 1906.
Authority is…|Wealth|Privilege|Power|Service|3|CCC 1897.
Participation is…|Useless|Dangerous|A right and duty|Optional|2|CCC 1913.
lessons.saint: Thomas More: the lawyer and statesman who told the truth to a king and died for his conscience.
misc: “Catholic social teaching belongs to one political party.”
“The Church should stay out of public life.”
lessons.mem: “So God created man in his own image.” (Genesis 1:27)
lessons.hook: Read Genesis 1:27. Ask: “How does this verse apply to laws about work, housing, health?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to define the common good and subsidiarity and apply them to a case.

lessons.title: Solidarity and the poor
lessons.idea: Solidarity is the firm commitment to the good of all, because we are responsible for one another. The preferential love for the poor reflects Christ’s identification with them: “As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.”
lessons.question: What is the option for the poor?
lessons.activity: “Service reflection” (40 min). Students plan and carry out (or reflect on) a service experience: serving a meal, tutoring, visiting the elderly. They reflect: What did I see? Who is invisible? What is one structural cause and one personal action?
teach: Solidarity is a social virtue and Christian love (CCC 1939–1942). John Paul II: not “a feeling of vague compassion” but “a firm and persevering determination to commit oneself to the common good.”
The preferential option for the poor (CCC 2443–2449): the poor are first in God’s love, and works of mercy are required (CCC 2447).
Charity and justice go together: giving to the poor is “a duty of justice” (CCC 2446). Almsgiving, volunteering and advocacy are all needed.
Pope Francis: “a Church that is poor and for the poor.”
quiz: Solidarity is…|Sentiment|Politics|Charity only|Commitment to the common good|3|CCC 1939.
The poor are…|Unimportant|Burdens|Lazy|Close to Christ|3|CCC 2448.
Matthew 25 says what we do to the least…|Is private|Is optional|We do to Christ|Doesn’t matter|2|Matthew 25:40.
lessons.saint: Vincent de Paul: a priest who organized charity for the poor and founded the Vincentians.
misc: “Poverty is always the poor person’s fault.”
lessons.mem: “As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” (Matthew 25:40)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 25:31–46. Ask: “What is the criterion of the final judgment? What surprised the people?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain solidarity and the preferential option for the poor with an example.

lessons.title: Creation and stewardship
lessons.idea: God entrusted creation to us as stewards. We must care for it with respect for its integrity, for the good of all and for future generations. Laudato Si’ calls for an “integral ecology” linking care for creation with care for the poor.
lessons.question: How can we care for creation?
lessons.activity: “Environmental project” (45 min). Students plan and start a project: reduce waste at school, plant a garden, organize a clean-up, audit energy use. Define goal, steps, partners and a prayer. Include reading excerpts from Laudato Si’.
teach: Creation is a gift with its own goodness (CCC 339–341). The seventh commandment requires respect for the integrity of creation (CCC 2415–2418).
Animals are to be treated kindly but not equal to persons (CCC 2416–2418). Resources are for all, now and in the future.
Laudato Si’ (2015) calls for “ecological conversion,” links environmental degradation with injustice to the poor and asks for lifestyle changes (the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor).
St Francis of Assisi is patron of ecology. The Canticle of the Creatures is a good prayer.
quiz: Genesis 2:15 says humans should…|Ignore|Till and keep the garden|Destroy|Rule|1|Genesis 2:15.
Laudato Si’ is by…|Benedict XVI|John Paul II|Francis|Leo XIII|2|2015.
Stewardship is…|Waste|Care for God’s gifts|Use|Ownership|1|CCC 2415.
lessons.saint: Francis of Assisi: who gave up wealth to follow Christ in poverty and joy and wrote the Canticle of the Creatures.
misc: “Dominion means we can use creation however we like.”
lessons.mem: “The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to till it and keep it.” (Genesis 2:15)
lessons.hook: Read Genesis 2:15 (“to till it and keep it”). Ask: “What does it mean to be a gardener, not an owner?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain Catholic stewardship and propose a concrete action.

units.title: Hard questions: marriage, family and suffering
units.eq: How does the Church walk with people in difficult situations?

lessons.title: Divorce and annulment
lessons.idea: Marriage is a permanent bond. The Church does not recognize divorce as ending a valid marriage, but an annulment can declare that a valid marriage never existed, and divorced Catholics are still part of the Church.
lessons.question: Is annulment just Catholic divorce?
lessons.activity: Study the steps of an annulment and the questions a tribunal asks.
teach: Jesus taught that what God has joined together no one should separate (Mark 10:9; CCC 2382). A valid, consummated sacramental marriage can be dissolved only by death (CCC 1638–1640).

An annulment is a finding that the marriage was never valid, for example because of a lack of freedom, serious incapacity or intention (CCC 1629). It does not make children illegitimate and is not a verdict on blame.

Divorced Catholics are not excommunicated. Those who remarry without an annulment cannot receive Communion, but the Church asks that they be welcomed, prayed for and helped (CCC 1651; Amoris Laetitia, 2016).
Separation may be necessary for safety (CCC 1649), especially in cases of abuse. The Church never asks someone to stay in danger.
talk: What are the risks to a family when marriage is treated as temporary?
Why might someone feel judged by the Church after a divorce?
How can a parish accompany people in broken marriages?
quiz: What does an annulment declare?|That a valid marriage never existed|That children are illegitimate|That one spouse is guilty|That a marriage has ended|0|CCC 1629.
A divorced Catholic who has not remarried…|May receive the sacraments|Must leave the Church|May not attend Mass|Is excommunicated|0|CCC 1651.
When may spouses separate?|Only with a bishop’s permission|Never|When necessary, such as for safety|When they disagree|2|CCC 1649.
lessons.life: Pray for a family you know that is struggling. Offer practical help.
lessons.saint: Monica: a mother who prayed for decades for her husband and her son Augustine.
misc: “An annulment is just a Catholic divorce.”

lessons.title: Same-sex attraction and the Church’s teaching
lessons.idea: The Church teaches that every person has dignity and must be treated with respect, compassion and sensitivity, and that marriage is a lifelong union of one man and one woman. It calls people with same-sex attraction to chastity.
lessons.question: How can the Church say both “love everyone” and “marriage is man and woman”?
lessons.activity: Write a short guide: how to talk with a friend who is gay and a Christian.
teach: Sensitive topic: some students are living this. Teach clearly, charitably and without humiliating anyone; let students step out; never ask a student to “out” themselves.

The Catechism says homosexual persons “must be accepted with respect, compassion, and sensitivity. Every sign of unjust discrimination in their regard should be avoided” (CCC 2358). Same-sex attraction itself is not a sin. Acts are held to be contrary to the natural law (CCC 2357), and persons are called to chastity (CCC 2359).
Marriage, in Catholic teaching, is the lifelong union of a man and a woman, open to children (CCC 1601). The Church’s teaching does not allow it to bless same-sex marriage as a sacrament.

Many people find this teaching very painful. A good response listens, does not mock or condemn, and affirms that every person is made in God’s image and loved by God. Bullying has no place in a Catholic school.
talk: What does it mean to “accept with respect, compassion and sensitivity”?
Why can disagreeing with someone’s choice still be done with love?
What would it take for a parish to feel safe for everyone?
quiz: What does CCC 2358 say about people with same-sex attraction?|They are excommunicated|They cannot be baptized|They must be treated with respect, compassion and sensitivity|They should be avoided|2|CCC 2358.
Is same-sex attraction itself a sin?|No, the Church distinguishes attraction from acts|Yes, always|The Church has no teaching|Only for clergy|0|CCC 2358–2359.
In Catholic teaching, marriage is…|Any loving relationship|A temporary contract|A matter of civil law only|A lifelong union of a man and a woman|3|CCC 1601.
lessons.life: Ask yourself: have I ever laughed at a joke that hurt someone? Choose to stop and apologize if you need to.
lessons.saint: Philip Neri: a priest of joy and mercy who welcomed everyone, including those on the margins.
misc: “The Church teaches that being gay is a sin.”

lessons.title: Euthanasia, suicide and caring for the dying
lessons.idea: Life is a gift to be received, so the Church rejects euthanasia and assisted suicide, yet it also does not require extraordinary treatments and strongly supports palliative care and accompaniment of the dying.
lessons.question: What is the difference between letting someone die and killing?
lessons.activity: Interview a hospice worker or read about palliative care.
teach: Sensitive topic: some students have lost a loved one to suicide or illness. Provide resources and use gentle language.

Euthanasia, acts or omissions that by their nature or intention cause death to end suffering, is morally unacceptable (CCC 2277). The Church distinguishes this from stopping treatments that are burdensome or disproportionate (CCC 2278) and from pain relief even if it shortens life (CCC 2279).

Suicide is gravely contrary to love of self and God (CCC 2280–2281), yet mental illness, fear and anguish may lessen responsibility, and “we should not despair of the eternal salvation of persons who have taken their own lives” (CCC 2282–2283).
If you or someone you know is in crisis, tell a trusted adult and call or text 988 (in the U.S.). The Church’s answer to suffering is accompaniment and care.
talk: What is the difference between refusing a burdensome treatment and killing a patient?
Why does the Church say pain relief is good?
What can a community do for someone who is dying or who feels they are a burden?
quiz: The Church teaches that euthanasia is…|A matter of choice|Only wrong for Catholics|Morally unacceptable|Required in some cases|2|CCC 2277.
Which of these is allowed?|Directly causing death to end suffering|Refusing disproportionate or burdensome treatment|Withholding food and water to cause death|Assisted suicide|1|CCC 2278.
CCC 2283 says…|Prayer for them is forbidden|Such people are certainly lost|They may not be mentioned|We should not despair of the salvation of those who have taken their own lives|3|God knows hearts.
lessons.life: Make a card for someone in a nursing home or hospice, and know the number 988.
lessons.saint: Cicely Saunders: a Christian who founded the modern hospice movement.
misc: “The Church says every possible medical treatment must always be used.”
“A person who dies by suicide is automatically lost forever.”
